title: Anand Sahib
hookLine: Guru Amar Das's song of bliss, part of the morning or evening prayers
last: YOUR SIMRAN · NITNEM · JAPJI · JAAP · SAVAIYAS · CHAUPAI.

lines: A WEDDING, A NAMING, A MEMORIAL.
THE SAME SONG NEAR THE END.
cards: A wedding. A child's naming. A memorial.
An ordinary Sunday service. Four very different mornings in a gurdwara, and near the end of each one, the same short song.

The Sikh code of conduct asks for it at the close of services, so it's sung over happy occasions and sad ones alike, and then everyone stands for the prayer called Ardas. It's the song of bliss, written by the third Guru.

teach.b: Anand means bliss, deep joy. Anand Sahib is by Guru Amar Das, the third Guru, and it's in the Guru Granth Sahib in Raag Ramkali: forty pauris.
Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite all forty in the morning, after Chaupai.

A shorter form, the first five pauris and the last, is sung at the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, and part of it is said in the evening Rehras too. The first line is where the whole song lives.

teach.h: JOY HAS COME, O MY MOTHER.
teach.b: In paraphrase: joy has come, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru. Notice who the line is spoken to. Not a crowd.
O my mother. It sounds like someone bursting through the kitchen door with news. And notice the tense.
Joy has come. Not a wish: something that happened.

The line goes on to say the Guru was found with sahaj, with ease, naturally, and that the heart is filled with music. Then the pauris turn the joy over, the way you'd turn a stone in your hand. What is real joy?
Everyone talks about bliss, the song says, but bliss is known through the Guru. True anand comes from the Name and the Guru's word, and the song asks the listener to sing that word.
So this bliss isn't the same as having no troubles.
That's how it can be sung at funerals as well as weddings: the joy sits underneath, a sense of having been found.
Tradition says Guru Amar Das found his Guru late, when he was already in his sixties. Joy, found, even then.

how: Sikhs who keep the five-bani Nitnem recite all forty pauris of Anand Sahib in the morning; its short form of six pauris is sung near the close of Sikh services and ceremonies, before Ardas.

o: Guru Amar Das's song of deep joy
a lullaby for putting children to sleep
a battle cry for going into war

games.q: what's inside Anand Sahib — tap the pairs.
p: the third Guru, who wrote it

s: Anand Sahib is sung only at weddings
its short form closes Sikh services and ceremonies, joyful or sad.
the first line is spoken to 'my mother'
joy has come, O my mother, for I have found the true Guru.
in Raag Ramkali, in the Guru Granth Sahib.

games.q: it's a memorial service. the family is grieving. near the end, what does the sangat sing?
o: nothing: songs of joy don't belong here.
the short form of Anand Sahib, the song of bliss.
a lament written for funerals only.
games.why: Anand is sung at funerals as well as weddings. its joy isn't the absence of trouble but a steadier sense of having been found.

practice: If you can, play about a minute of Anand Sahib's first pauri and let the opening line land: joy has come, O my mother. If not, remember a moment you ran to tell someone good news: who you told, and how it felt to say it out loud.
Sit inside that moment, then let it settle into something quieter.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: anand, bliss; the title of Guru Amar Das's hymn.

carryVoice: Your line: joy, found. Joy has come, O my mother. Day one hundred thirty-three, and the morning set is whole.
